  MISSION STATEMENT
  The mission of the City of Monterey Park is to provide excellent services
  to enhance the quality of life for our entire community.

  LAND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
  We would like to acknowledge that the land we inhabit today was once known as
  Tovangaar, the home of the Gabrieleño-Tongva people. We show our respect to the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, as well as all Indigenous people, past, present, and future,
  and honor their labor as original caretakers of this land. We commit to uplifting the
  Gabrieleño-Tongva people, invite you to acknowledge the history, and join us in caring
  for this land.

GENERAL INFORMATION
Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at 320
West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s website
at http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/AgendaCenter/City-Council-17.

The public may watch the meeting live on the city’s cable channel MPKTV (AT&T U-verse, channel 99
or Charter Communications, channel 182) or by visiting the city’s website at
http://www.montereypark.ca.gov/133/City-Council-Meeting-Videos.Per the Americans with Disabilities
Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting, please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359
for reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a meeting. Council Chambers are wheelchair
accessible.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION
You may speak up to 5 minutes on Agenda item. You may combine up to 2 minutes of time with another
person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City Council
may change the amount of time allowed for speakers. Written Communication will be accepted up to 24
hours before the meeting via email to mpclerk@montereypark.ca.gov.

While all comments are welcome, the Brown Act does not allow the City Council to take action on any
item not on the agenda. The Council may briefly respond to comments after Public Communications is
closed. Persons may, in addition to any other matter within the City Council's subject-matter jurisdiction,
comment on Agenda Items at this time. If you provide public comment on a specific Agenda item at this
time, however, you cannot later provide comments at the time the Agenda Item is considered.

  SUBJECT: Consideration and possible action to adopt a Resolution to record a
  Notice of Nuisance Abatement Lien against certain real property in the
  City (APN 5254-002-031)

RECOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council:
  1. Adopt a resolution to record a Notice of Nuisance Abatement Lien; and/or
  2. Take such additional, related action that may be desirable.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):

Adoption of the Resolution is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act
(“CEQA”) under CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) because it can be seen with certainty
that there is no possibility that the action proposed by the proposed resolution would have
a significant effect on the environment.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

Adopting the attached resolution will allow the City to recover costs, including attorney’s
fees, incurred the City’s abatement of the public nuisance present on certain real property
located in the City (Lot 1 of Tract No. 34875—APN 5254-002-031) (the “Property”) owned
by Center Int’l Investments, Inc. (“CII”). The Resolution authorizes recording the
associated Notice of Nuisance Abatement Lien in the amount of $61,337.27. This will be
the seventh lien placed on the Property and covers expenses that the City incurred
between October 1, 2023, and December 31, 2023. After recording this lien, the liens
against the Property will total $15,838,317.43.

BACKGROUND AND DISCUSSION:

As the Council is aware, the City is abating the public nuisance on the Property in
accordance with the Settlement Agreement voluntarily entered into by CII in the civil case
captioned The People of the State of California, ex rel., Mark D. Hensley, City Attorney
for the City of Monterey Park v. Center Int’l Investments, Inc., et al. which was filed on
December 31, 2015 (LASC Case No. BC605788).

  Page 6 of 255
 Staff Report
Page 2
March 6, 2024

On May 4, 2022, and August 1, 2022, March 15, 2023, September 3, 2023, and January
17, 2024, the City authorized liens against the Property for nuisance abatement cost
recovery. On January 18, 2024, Management Services Director Martha Garcia sent
correspondence (Resolution Exhibit A) demanding CII’s payment of $61,337.27 to the
City in abatement costs for Quarter 4 of 2023. This is in addition to liens already placed
on the Property totaling $15,776,980.16. The City has not received any payments from
CII. After recording this lien, the liens against the Property will total $15,838,317.43.

Pursuant to MPMC § 4.30.150 and Government Code § 38773.1, the City may recover
its nuisance abatement costs by recording a lien against a Subject Property. The
attached Resolution authorizes the City to record a Notice of Nuisance Abatement Lien
against the Property. Under California law and upon recordation, the notice would
constitute a lien against the Property with the force, effect, and priority of a judgment
lien. The City can foreclose against the lien through an action for a money judgment.
CII previously agreed to waive its notice and hearing rights in § 7 of the First
Amendment to the Settlement Agreement.

FISCAL IMPACT:

The attached Resolution will allow the City to impose a lien on the Property in the
amount of $61,337.27. This is one of several notices that will be continuing being
brought to the City Council for consideration.

 Respectfully submitted by:

 ____________________________
  Justin A. Tamayo,
  Deputy City Attorney

 SUBJECT:  Annual Military Equipment Report Per Assembly Bill No. 481

RECOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Receiving and filing report; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

On May 18, 2022, the Monterey Park City Council adopted Ordinance No. 2222 approving
a Military Equipment Use Policy (Monterey Park Police Department – Policy 709)
pursuant to Assembly Bill No. 481 (“AB 481”). In accordance with AB 481 and Policy 709,
a military equipment report must be submitted to the City Council annually for each type
of military equipment approved within one year of approval, and annually thereafter for as
long as the military equipment is available for use. In compliance with AB 481, outlined
below is the 2023 MPPD Annual Military Equipment Report.

It is recommended the City Council approve the Annual Military Equipment Report per
Assembly Bill No. 481.

BACKGROUND:

Effective January 1, 2022, Assembly Bill 481 required law enforcement agencies such as
the Monterey Park Police Department (“MPPD”) to have a Military Equipment Use Policy
approved by the City Council prior to acquiring or using military equipment. The City
complied and adopted Ordinance No. 2222 approving Policy 709.

AB 481 requires law enforcement agencies to submit an annual military equipment report
on the use of the equipment, any complaint(s) or concern(s) regarding the use of the
equipment, results of any internal audits on the use of the equipment, the annual costs to
maintain the equipment, the quantity possessed by the agency and the law enforcement
agency’s intention to purchase additional equipment in the following year.

709.1 PURPOSE AND SCOPE
The purpose of this policy is to provide guidelines for the approval, acquisition, and reporting
requirements of military equipment (Government Code § 7070; Government Code § 7071;
Government Code § 7072).

709.1.1 DEFINITIONS
Definitions related to this policy include (Government Code § 7070):
Governing body – The elected or appointed body that oversees the Department.
Military equipment – Includes but is not limited to the following:
  •  Unmanned, remotely piloted, powered aerial or ground vehicles.
  •  Mine-resistant ambush-protected (MRAP) vehicles or armored personnel carriers.
  •  High mobility multipurpose wheeled vehicles (HMMWV), two-and-one-half-ton trucks,
  five-ton trucks, or wheeled vehicles that have a breaching or entry apparatus attached.
  •  Tracked armored vehicles that provide ballistic protection to their occupants.
  •  Command and control vehicles that are either built or modified to facilitate the
  operational control and direction of public safety units.
  •  Weaponized aircraft, vessels, or vehicles of any kind.
  •  Battering rams, slugs, and breaching apparatuses that are explosive in nature. This
  does not include a handheld, one-person ram.
  •  Firearms and ammunition of .50 caliber or greater, excluding standard-issue shotguns
  and standard-issue shotgun ammunition.
  •  Specialized firearms and ammunition of less than .50 caliber, including firearms and
  accessories identified as assault weapons in Penal Code § 30510 and Penal Code §
  30515, with the exception of standard-issue firearms.
  •  Any firearm or firearm accessory that is designed to launch explosive projectiles.
  •  Noise-flash diversionary devices and explosive breaching tools.
  •  Munitions containing tear gas or OC, excluding standard, service-issued handheld
  pepper spray.
  •  TASER® Shockwave, microwave weapons, water cannons, and long-range acoustic
  devices (LRADs).
  •  Kinetic energy weapons and munitions.
  •  Any other equipment as determined by a governing body or a state agency to require
  additional oversight.

709.2 APPROVAL OF THE GOVERNING BODY

The Chief of Police or his/her authorized designee shall seek approval for this policy from the
governing body in the form of an ordinance adopting the policy. As part of the approval seeking
process, the Chief of Police, or his/her authorized designee, will submit the proposed military
equipment policy to the governing body and make it available on the Department website at least
30 days prior to any public hearing concerning the military equipment at issue (Government Code
§ 7071).
The governing body must approve the policy prior to the Department or its members engaging in
any of the following (Government Code § 7071):
  (a)  Requesting military equipment made available pursuant to 10 USC § 2576a.
  (b)  Seeking funds for military equipment, including but not limited to applying for a grant,
  soliciting or accepting private, local, state, or federal funds, in-kind donations, or other
  donations or transfers.
  (c)  Acquiring military equipment either permanently or temporarily, including by borrowing
  or leasing.
  (d)  Collaborating with another law enforcement agency in the deployment or other use of
  military equipment within the jurisdiction of this department.
  (e)  Using any new or existing military equipment for a purpose, in a manner, or by a person
  not previously approved by the governing body.
  (f)  Soliciting or responding to a proposal for, or entering into an agreement with, any other
  person or entity to seek funds for, apply to receive, acquire, use, or collaborate in the
  use of military equipment.
  (g)  Acquiring military equipment through any means not provided above.

709.3 POLICY
The acquisition of military equipment and its deployment in our communities may impact the
public's safety and welfare. The public has a right to know about any funding, acquisition, or use of
military equipment by local government officials, as well as a right to participate in any government
agency's decision to fund, acquire, or use such equipment. Decisions whether and how to fund,
acquire, or use military equipment will be made with strong consideration for the public's welfare,
safety, civil rights, and civil liberties and also account for the public's input.
It is the policy of the Monterey Park Police Department that there are legally enforceable
safeguards, including transparency, oversight, and accountability measures in place to protect the
public's welfare, safety, civil rights, and civil liberties before military equipment is funded, acquired,
or used.
Members of the Monterey Park Police Department will only use military equipment in compliance
with federal and state legal authorities, including the Fourth and Fifth Amendments of the U.S.
Constitution; Article 1, Section 1 of the California Constitution; Government Code § 7286; and,

709.4 MILITARY EQUIPMENT COORDINATOR
The Chief of Police should designate a member of this department to act as the military equipment
coordinator. The responsibilities of the military equipment coordinator include but are not limited to:
  (a)  Acting as liaison to the governing body for matters related to the requirements of this
  policy.
  (b)  Identifying Department equipment that qualifies as "military equipment," as defined
  in Government Code § 7070, in the current possession of the Department, or the
  equipment the Department intends to acquire that requires approval by the governing
  body.
  (c)  Conducting an inventory of all military equipment at least annually.
  (d)  Collaborating with any allied agency that may use military equipment within the
  jurisdiction of Monterey Park Police Department (Government Code § 7071).
  (e)  Preparing for, scheduling, and coordinating the annual community engagement
  meeting to include:
  1.  Publicizing the details of the meeting.
  2.  Preparing for public questions regarding the department's funding, acquisition,
  and use of equipment.
  (f)  Preparing the annual military equipment report for submission to the Chief of Police
  and ensuring that the report is made available on the department website (Government
  Code § 7072).
  (g)  Receive and timely respond to public concerns, complaints, or questions regarding
  the use of military equipment.

709.7 COORDINATION WITH OTHER JURISDICTIONS
Police Department will not collaborate with other law enforcement agencies to use military
equipment in this jurisdiction unless the military equipment is approved for use, and used in
accordance with this policy.

709.8 ANNUAL REPORT
Upon approval of a military equipment policy, the Chief of Police or the authorized designee should
submit a military equipment report to the governing body for each type of military equipment
approved within one year of approval, and annually thereafter for as long as the military equipment
is available for use (Government Code § 7072).
The Chief of Police or the authorized designee should also make each annual military equipment
report publicly available on the department website for as long as the military equipment is
available for use. The report will include all information required by Government Code § 7072 for
the preceding calendar year for each type of military equipment in department inventory.

709.9 COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT
Within 30 days of submitting and publicly releasing the annual report, the Department shall hold
at least one well-publicized and conveniently located community engagement meeting, at which
the Department should discuss the report and respond to public questions regarding the funding,
acquisition, or use of military equipment.

 SUBJECT:  Amendment to Professional Service Agreement No. (“PSA”) 2303-AB
  For Consultant Services Related To Industrial Waste, And Fats, Oils And
  Grease (“FOG”) Management And Control Programs

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Authorizing the City Manager to execute a Second Amendment to Agreement
  2303-AB with John L. Hunter & Associates for Industrial Waste and FOG
  Management and Control Program Assistance, in a form approved by the City
  Attorney; and
  2. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
Staff recommends the City Council approve a Second Amendment to Agreement 2303-
AB with John L. Hunter & Associates for the addition of Industrial Waste Program and
FOG management and control assistance services.

BACKGROUND:
The California State Water Resources Board’s Waste Discharge Requirements Order for
Sanitary Sewer Systems requires all cities in California to develop and implement a Sewer
System Management Plan. The plan documents a City’s procedures to properly operate
and maintain its sewer system. One component of the plan is the Industrial Waste (“IW”)
Program, which regulates facilities that generate industrial wastewater that is released
into the City’s sewer system. The goal of an IW program is to manage the sewage to
prevent the discharge of pollution to surface and groundwater.

Since 1983, the City of Monterey Park has contracted with the County of Los Angeles
(“County”) for IW inspections. Currently, the City of Monterey Park has an estimated 66
IW permitted facilities. As part of the IW program process, a facility must submit a plan
check application and have its facility inspected to ensure full compliance. Given the size
and jurisdiction of the County, staff has seen a decrease in the level of service towards
IW inspections, plan checks and responsiveness to business owners throughout the
process. Similarly, there has been a disconnect in relaying the status of IW inspections
to City employees. Given the current issues, staff is recommending amending the City’s

current contract with John L. Hunter & Associates (“JLHA”) to include the
administration and implementation of the City’s Industrial Waste Program.

Currently, JLHA provides the City with commercial stormwater inspections for
compliance with the State National Pollution Discharge Elimination System
(“NPDES”), under stormwater relations, as well as FOG program assistance services.

While JLHA currently provides FOG services, those services need to be amended
to reflect a greater number of noncompliant facilities in the City which requires
JLHA to provide more services. The existing JLHA agreement assumed compliance
inspections would find that approximately 10% of facilities were noncompliant with the
FOG program. However, inspections have revealed that the number of
noncompliant facilities is approximately 48% which has resulted in an increase in the
amount of follow up services that JLHA must provide to ensure program compliance.

Additionally, JLHA is prepared to add IW program assistance to its scope of
work including inspections, follow-up activities and outreach education. In moving the
City’s IW program assistance to JLHA, staff anticipates a more uniform and
thorough inspection process, as well as a more direct line of communication and
oversight into the IW Program. To align with JLHA’s current agreement with
the City, its services will be conducted through 2026-2027.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The City collects an annual inspection fee as part of its IW Program. These
revenues offset the IW Program and FOG Program costs. Services for this
Amendment will begin July 1, 2024, and funds will be budgeted in the proposed Fiscal
Year 2024-2025 Budget. The total proposed FY2024-2025 cost for the IW Program and
FOG Program with JLHA will not exceed $64,280.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
It is recommended that City Council waive the fare to the Spirit Bus on Monday, April 22,
2024, when Earth Day will be celebrated globally. Free rides on the Spirit Bus will
promote public transportation and reduce traffic and the City’s carbon footprint through
the reduction of automobile emissions. This action will support the City’s Going Green
initiative to encourage the community to consider environmentally friendly activities such
as using alternative forms of transportation. The Spirit Bus fare was also waived last year
in honor of Earth Day 2023.

2023-2024 STRATEGIC PLAN GOAL:
Waiving the Spirit Bus fare – in addition to being de minimis – helps the City meet its the
sustainability goal.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The Spirit Bus fare is $0.25 per passenger per boarding. Based on the most current
ridership data, there are an average of 218 Spirit Bus boardings on Mondays. The fiscal
impact of waiving bus fares in honor of Earth Day is approximately $54.50. This revenue
loss will be from General Funds.

 SUBJECT:  Annual Weed Abatement Protest Hearing

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Opening the public hearing, receiving public comment, closing the public hearing;
  2. Adopting a Resolution declaring that weeds, brush, rubbish and refuse upon or in
  front of specified property in the city are a seasonal and recurrent public
  nuisance, and declaring its intention to provide for abatement; and/or
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act):
Adoption of this Resolution is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act
(“CEQA”) under CEQA Guidelines § 15061(b)(3) because it can be seen with certainty
that there is no possibility that the Resolution may have a significant effect on the
environment.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The County of Los Angeles Department of Agriculture Commissioner/Weights and
Measures (Weed Abatement Division) submitted to the City the annual Weed Abatement
Declaration List and resolution declaring that weeds, brush, rubbish, refuse and dirt
maintained on certain private properties in the City are a public nuisance. At the regular
City Council meeting on February 21, 2024, the Council adopted Resolution No. 2024-
R9 approving the 2024 Weed Abatement Declaration List as posted by the County.
By adopting the Resolution, the Council declared its intention to provide for the
abatement of said public nuisances. To complete the process, the Council must
hold a protest hearing to allow parcel owners identified on the Declaration List an
opportunity to object to their inclusion thereon.

BACKGROUND:
The County identified 1,610 improved and unimproved parcels requiring abatement in the
2024 Declaration List. The County mailed notices on or about January 4, 2024 to the
recorded owner of each parcel included in the list declaring that their parcel is an existing,
future, or “potential” hazard. The County advised that it considers a parcel a future or
“potential” hazard if the parcel is not completely landscaped or irrigated and there is a

  Page 87 of 255
 Staff Report
Page 2 of 3
March 6, 2024

potential for weed growth. The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors established an
inspection fee of $51.59 for the 2024 abatement cycle.

Parcel owners who received notices from the County can challenge their parcels inclusion
on the list by attending the protest hearing. Parcel can request Council to remove their
parcels from the list if they feel that their parcel is not in violation or that the County as
erred by including the parcel on the list. The City Manager also has the authority to
remove parcels from the list, thus the City Council may defer any requests for removal to
the City Manager for further consideration.

The County advised staff that if parcel owners want their parcel to be removed from the
Declaration List, the County will conduct re-inspection of the parcel to determine if, in fact,
the parcel is not in violation or a potential hazard, or that an error has been made. Upon
completion of the re-inspection of the parcel, the County will advise the City of its findings.
When a parcel is re-inspected and found to be in violation or a potential hazard, the
County will remove the parcel from the deletion list. The deletion list will allow the re-
inspection fee of $51.59 to be waived.

The County advised the City that March 13, 2024 is the last day that the City can request
or the County can authorize removal of a parcel from the Declaration List. If the City
Council elects to remove a parcel from the Declaration List and the parcel becomes a
nuisance at a later date, the City will have to place that parcel on an individual declaration
list and will have to hold an individual protest hearing for each parcel.

The following is a schedule of the Weed Abatement process:

March 13, 2024  Deadline for the City to authorize removal of a property from the
  Declaration List

April 2, 2024  County will begin clearance operations on unimproved (vacant)
  parcels.

May 15, 2024  Deadline for all improved parcels to attain compliance that
  responded to the County via response cards. County will begin
  compliance inspections.

August 7, 2024  Weed Abatement Charge List Hearing of Weed Abatement Costs
  directing the County to collect these costs through property tax
  billings.

FISCAL IMPACT:
The City of Monterey Park has been contracting with the County of Los Angeles since
1992 for weed abatement services. No fiscal impacts are anticipated to affect actual
expenditures or revenues. Furthermore, no redirection of available staff time, supplies or
services will be required.

  A RESOLUTION ADOPTED PURSUANT TO GOVERNMENT
  CODE § 39561 DECLARING THAT WEEDS, BRUSH, RUBBISH
  AND REFUSE UPON OR IN FRONT OF SPECIFIED PROPERTY
  IN THE CITY ARE A SEASONAL AND RECURRENT PUBLIC
  NUISANCE, AND DECLARING ITS INTENTION TO PROVIDE FOR
  ABATEMENT

The City Council does resolve as follows:

SECTION 1:  Pursuant to Government Code §§ 39500 to 39588, and evidence
received by it, the City Council finds and declares that:

  A.  The weeds or brush growing or existing upon the streets and sidewalks in
  front of those properties identified in attached Exhibit “A” have attained such
  large growth as to become, when dry, a fire menace to adjacent improved
  property, or which are otherwise noxious, dangerous, or a public nuisance;

  B.  The presence of dry grass, stubble, refuse, or other flammable materials
  are conditions which endanger the public safety by creating a fire hazard;
  and

  C.  By reason of the foregoing fact, the weeds, brush, rubbish, dry grass,
  stubble, refuse, or other flammable material growing or existing upon the
  private property identified in Exhibit “A”, or upon the streets and sidewalks
  in front of said property constitute a seasonal and recurrent public nuisance
  (as defined by applicable law including, without limitation Monterey Park
  Municipal Code §§ 4.30.040 and 4.30.050(j)) and should be abated before
  the coming fire season.

SECTION 2:  Pursuant to the findings outlined in Section 1, the Agricultural
Commissioner/Director of Weights and Measures, County of Los Angeles, is designated
to give notice to destroy said weeds, brush, rubbish, dry grass, stubble, refuse, or other
flammable material and will cause notices to be given to each property owner by United
States Mail and said notice must be substantially in the following form:

  “NOTICE TO DESTROY WEEDS,
  REMOVE BRUSH, RUBBISH AND REFUSE

  Notice is hereby given that on March 6, 2024, the City Council of the City of
  Monterey Park adopted a resolution declaring noxious or dangerous
  vegetation including weeds, brush, tumbleweeds, sagebrush or rubbish
  and refuse were growing or occurring upon or in front of said property on
  certain streets in said city or unincorporated area of the County of Los

  Angeles, and more particularly described in the resolution, and that they
  constitute a public nuisance which must be abated by the removal of said
  noxious or dangerous vegetation, rubbish and refuse. The resolution
  further declares that, if not abated, the vegetation and/or rubbish and
  refuse may be removed and the nuisance abated by County authorities in
  which case the cost of removal will be assessed upon the land from or in
  front of which the noxious or dangerous vegetation, rubbish and refuse
  are removed. Such cost will constitute a special assessment against such
  lots or lands. Reference is hereby made to said resolution for further
  particulars. In addition, the City Council for Monterey Park authorized and
  directed the Agricultural Commissioner to recover its costs of details.

  Maychelle Yee, City Clerk, City of Monterey Park”

SECTION 3:  Costs. All costs associated with implementing this Resolution
including, without limitation, costs incurred by the Agricultural Commissioner for
inspecting the Properties, may be recovered in accordance with City or County
resolutions. Recovering these costs is vital to the ongoing operation governing the
identification and abatement of those properties that constitute a seasonal and recurrent
public nuisance and endanger the public safety. The Agricultural Commissioner is
authorized and directed to recover its costs of inspection of the properties hereinabove
described in a manner consistent with prior action of the Board adopting a fee schedule
for such inspections. The Agricultural Commissioner or authorities from the County of Los
Angeles must keep an itemized written account of the cost of abatement. A copy of these
accounts will be available for inspection at the City Clerk’s Office located at 320 W.
Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754 for at least three days before August 21,
2024.

SECTION 4:  Reliance on Record. Every one of the findings and determinations in
this Resolution are based on the competent and substantial evidence, both oral and
written, contained in the entire record relating to the project. The findings and
determinations constitute the independent findings and determinations of the City Council
in all respects and are fully and completely supported by substantial evidence in the
record as a whole.

SECTION 5:  Summaries of Information. All summaries of information in the
findings, which precede this section, are based on the substantial evidence in the record.
The absence of any particular fact from any such summary is not an indication that a
particular finding is not based in part on that fact.

SECTION 6:  Severability. lf any part of this Resolution or its application is deemed
invalid by a court of competent jurisdiction, the City Council intends that such invalidity
will not affect the effectiveness of the remaining provisions or applications and, to this
end, the provisions of this Resolution are severable.

 FROM:  Inez Alvarez, City Manager
 SUBJECT:  Discussion and direction regarding Assembly Bill 2979 (2024) (“AB
  2979”)

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Discussing and providing direction on AB 2979 entitled “Income taxation:
  exclusion: victim compensation” (an act relating to taxation);
  2. If desirable, signing a letter on behalf of the City either in support of or opposition
  to AB 2979; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
At the Regular City Council Meeting on February 21, 2024, the City Council requested a
discussion of AB 2979 be placed on a future City Council agenda. AB 2979 is attached
as Attachment 1, which contains the proposed law that was introduced by Assembly
Member Mike Fong. As of the writing of this staff report, AB 2979 solely consists of
establishing a legislative intent to pass subsequent legislation relating to the exclusion of
compensation received from the California Victim Compensation Board (CalVCB) from
the definition of gross income for the purpose of taxation.

BACKGROUND:
The CalVCB is a three-member board that is dedicated to assisting victims of violent
crimes. CalVCB currently administers the Victim Compensation Program which provides
reimbursement for crime-related expenses to victims who suffer physical injury or the
threat of physical injury as a result of a violent crime. Covered expenses by CalVCB
include, without limitation, funeral and burial costs, mental health services, and income
loss which aid in the recovery process.

While the Internal Revenue Service (“IRS”) policy exempts victim compensation funds
from federal taxes, current California law is unclear as to whether CalVCB funds are
subject to state taxes. If enacted, AB 2979 would establish a legislative intent to enact
subsequent legislation to that may exempt those who qualify for CalVCB payments from
state income taxes.

 TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council

 SUBJECT:  Discussion and direction regarding Senate Bill 1094 (2024) (“SB 1094”)

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council consider:
  1. Discussing and providing direction on SB 1094 entitled “Pupil instruction: course
  of study: social sciences: civic engagement” (an act to amend Sections 51210 and
  51220 of the Education Code, relating to pupil instruction);
  2. If desirable, signing a letter on behalf of the City either in support of or opposition
  to SB 1094; and
  3. Taking such additional, related, action that may be desirable.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
At the Regular City Council Meeting on February 21, 2024, the City Council requested a
discussion of SB 1094 be placed on a future City Council agenda. SB 1094 is attached
as Attachment 1, which contains the proposed law that was introduced by Senator
Monique Limón. If enacted, the amendment would require principles of democracy and
State and Federal constitutions to be taught to students in grade levels 1 through 12 and
also require a civic engagement or experience with a governmental institution at least
once between the grade levels of 1 through 6 and at least once between grade levels 7
through 8.

BACKGROUND:
Sections 51210 and 51220 of the Education Code were enacted by the California State
Legislature in 1976 which required adopted study areas for students in grade levels 1
through 12 including social sciences. Under the existing law, schools are required to teach
social sciences including the history, resources, development, and government of
California and the United States of America.

If enacted, SB 1094 would explicitly require instruction in social sciences to also include
principles of democracy and the State and Federal Constitutions. In addition, SB 1094
would require students to (at least once in grade levels 1 through 6 and at least once in
grade levels 7 through 8) complete a civic engagement or experience with a governmental
institution at the local, state, or national level.

policies and programs that help achieve goals contained within the General Plan.

BACKGROUND:
The City of Monterey Park’s last comprehensive update to the General Plan occurred in
2001 and contained seven elements that met California Government Code Section
65302, addressing land use, circulation, housing, noise, safety, conservation and open
space. Since that time, additional amendments to the General Plan have included:
  • New Sustainable Community Element (2014);
  • New Healthy Community Element (2014);
  • Updated Land Use Element (2019);
  • Updated Safety and Community Services Element (2022);
  • New Environmental Justice Element (2022); and
  • Updated Housing Element (2022);

The following sections provide an update of the status and implementation of each
element of the Monterey Park General Plan.

Land Use Element
A comprehensive update to the Land Use Element was adopted in 2019 and approved
by voters in November 2020. Since this time, the City has processed a variety of new land
use developments and adopted new land use regulations that have continually upheld
the Land Use Element. The following ordinances were initiated and adopted in 2023
related to land uses:
  • Outdoor dining regulations;
  • Firearm protection zone; and
  • Medical marijuana delivery consistent with SB 1186.

City Council has prioritized fixing inconsistencies between the Land Use Element and the
Monterey Park Municipal Code (“MPMC”) which implements the Land Use Element. In
Fall of 2023, the Community Development Department launched the Our City, Our Plan
campaign to make changes to zoning and update the MPMC to harmonize the General
Plan and the MPMC with the intention of igniting downtown revitalization, expand housing
opportunities and streamline development. In September 2023, the City held a public
workshop with residents and property owners to provide insight on the changes
addressing the inconsistencies between two documents. The first set of zone changes to
bring the City’s zoning into consistency with the Land Use Map were approved in late
2023. Work is ongoing on the Our City, Our Plan effort in 2024.

Economic Development Element
The Economic Development Element, last updated in 2001, helps guide City efforts to
maintain an economically viable range of housing and employment opportunities that
meet the needs of residents and workers. In 2023, City Council authorized an update of
the Economic Development Strategic Plan (which was last updated in 2010) and the City
hired a consulting firm to complete the process. An Economic Development Taskforce of
stakeholders was created and the first series of meetings occurred in late 2023 to help
shape the strategic plan’s update, which is slated for completion in the third quarter of
2024.

Last year, strides were made towards helping local small businesses in the following
areas:
  • Assisted businesses and non-profit organizations in obtaining low-interest federal
  disaster loans (7 loans/ $924,000+);
  • Facilitated $5,000 grants to small business through the Restaurants Care
  Resilience Fund (5 awards); and
  • Connected businesses with $2,500 micro-grants from the Latino Restaurant
  Association (3 awards).

To capitalize on the City’s initial success with connecting small businesses to funding
opportunities, a new feature was introduced in both digital and printed formats called

“Business Connect”. This monthly newsletter allows the City to showcase individual
businesses, provides useful information to business owners such as grant opportunities
and new laws that may affect business, or other areas of interest for small business
owners.

Circulation Element
The purpose of the Circulation Element, last updated in 2001, is to define a safe, efficient,
and adequate circulation system in the City that responds to all circulation needs. The
element also focuses on identification and evaluation of local circulation needs, while
balancing those needs with regional circulation, public transportation, and bicycle and
pedestrian circulation in the Monterey Park community.

The City has continued to make a variety of street and traffic improvements to its existing
network of public streets and sidewalks including street resurfacing, sidewalk repair,
Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) compliance, installation of bike lanes, and traffic
signal modifications.

These street and traffic improvements are identified as Capital Improvement Projects
(CIPs) in which federal, state and local funding sources are utilized to execute the
projects. Some of the projects completed in 2023 include 21.2 miles of streets resurfaced
and large slurry seal project of several residential neighborhoods. Additional
improvements to the circulation system related to traffic signals and sidewalk repairs
occurred at key intersections. Further, the Public Works Department published an
interactive map on the City’s website to show the location of CIPs to better track and notify
the public about such activities.

Related to transit services, the City launched the Passio Go! App to provide transit riders
with real-time status Spirit Bus routes by tracking arrival times and planning trips through
riders’ personal electronic devices. Enhancements to Spirit Bus operations include the
return of Route 5, which connects the nearby Metrolink stations at California State
University, Los Angeles (Cal State LA) and East Los Angeles City College’s (ELAC)
Transit Center and the LINK shuttle that provides connectivity to the Cal State LA Metro
Station and Corporate Center Drive. Additionally, hours of operation for the Spirit Bus and
the LINK shuttle were extended. The City continues to monitor and respond to the transit
needs of its users and citizens.

Housing Element
The Housing Element underwent a comprehensive update in 2022 and HCD certification
occurred in March 2023. The Element describes actions the City took and will take to
meet existing and future housing needs during the 6th Regional Housing Needs Allocation
(RHNA) cycle which runs between 2021-2029. The Housing Element outlines existing
and proposed housing programs and text amendments that are needed to meet statutory
requirements. The implementation of the housing programs was ongoing throughout the
planning cycle.

In the past year, the City worked on implementation of the Housing Element in order to

  • Updated Density Bonus Ordinance (Program 14); and

Additionally, the City became a member of the San Gabriel Valley Regional Housing Trust

planning and construction of homeless housing, and extremely low, very low and low-
income housing projects. In joining SGVRT, the City better positioned to take advantage
of funding opportunities as projects develop in the City.

Safety and Community Services Element
A comprehensive update to the Safety Element was completed in 2022. Throughout
2023, staff conducted and completed trainings related to national disasters including
trainings through the Standardized Emergency Management System (SEMS) and the
National Incident Management System (NIMS). Trainings have also engaged the
community through the Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) and
Neighborhood Watch programs.

The latest adoption of the Safety Element also prioritized climate change and seismic
hazards. To better address climate change, the Monterey Park Going Green program
continued throughout 2023 which included outreach and education and will result in the
development of a sustainability plan which will identify programs to mitigate climate
change and adapt to climate change that is already occurring.

Additionally, the City began efforts to update its Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) in
November 2022. The LHMP assesses local hazard vulnerabilities and identify mitigation
actions that the City will pursue to reduce impacts in the case of a hazard. In October

2023, the City provided a second draft of the LHMP for public review and comments.
Once the new plan is adopted by the City Council and approved by the Federal
Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the City will be eligible for Hazard Mitigation
Grant Program (HMGP) and other mitigation-related funding.

Resources Element
The Resources Element, last updated in 2001, addresses open space and conservation.
Because Monterey Park is a built-out urban community, there are few “natural” resources
such as forests or wildlife habitat or agricultural land. The Resources Element, therefore,
directs policy toward preserving those resources important in the urban environment of
Monterey Park and critical to preserving this City’s heritage for future generations. These
resources include City parks and other improved open space areas, historic resources,
water resources, and air quality. To further the goals within the Resources Element, staff
has diligently worked to preserve, enhance, and upgrade open space areas such as the
updates and upgrades to playground equipment throughout the City. The following
improvements were completed in 2023 to various City parks and facilities:
  • Sierra Vista Park – pickleball and basketball courts renovation and resurfacing;
  • George Elder Park – new mural, indoor restroom and fire alarm upgrades;
  • Edison Trails Park – new playground installation; and
  • Barnes Park Amphitheater – seating replacement.

Other efforts begun in 2023 and completed in 2024 include:
  • Sequoia Park – new playground installation;
  • Bella Vista Park – new playground installation; and
  • Garvey Ranch Park - new playground updates.

Maintenance and upgrade of the City’s open space facilities are an on-going extension of
Capital Improvement projects that the City carries out.

Healthy Community Element
A Healthy Community Element was adopted in 2014 and provides goals and policies to
guide City’s efforts to support and promote a healthier community by “making the healthy
choice the easy choice” for every community member. In 2023, the City provided free
COVID test kits which were distributed at Barnes Park, Bruggemeyer Library, and the
Langley Senior Center. The community was also able to benefit from free health clinics,
flu shots, and COVID-19 vaccines. The City has partnered with service providers through
the LA County Department of Health and Chinatown Service Center, among others to
offer these services free to residents.

Mental health also became a key area of focus in 2023. After the City’s mass shooting
incident in February, the City and its partners sought and provided mental health services
to those who were directly and indirectly impacted by the event, including victims,
employees, and community members. The MPK Hope Resiliency Center was opened in
the Sierra Vista Park Community Center to provide mental health services. Ongoing drop-

Langely Senior Center.

Sustainable Community Element
A Sustainable Community Element was adopted in 2014. This element establishes goals
and policies to guide City efforts to become a more sustainable and resilient community
through changes to municipal operations and by promoting and supporting sustainable
behaviors of individual community members. The City held or partnered in events that
featured electronic waste disposal, document shredding, landscape chipping, tree
planting, compost giveaways, and ride-free public transportation days.

The Monterey Park Going Green program was introduced in 2022 and efforts to develop
a plan to help the City and its residents be resilient to climate change continued in 2023.
Outreach in 2023 included multiple public workshops held to gather input and educate
residents on best green practices. Additional work on the draft plan included multiple
public meetings and a special joint Planning Commission and Environmental Commission
meeting in November 2023. A public draft was made available in 2024 and is slated for
adoption later in the year, with implementation to follow.

Environmental Justice Element.
An Environmental Justice Element was added to the General Plan in 2022. The
Environmental Justice Element includes goals, policies, and objectives that aim to reduce
health risks to any identified disadvantaged communities, promote civic engagement, and
prioritize the needs of disadvantaged communities. Through 2022, the City has strived to
promote and provide the public opportunities with civic engagement including workshops.
Various community efforts have promoted civic engagement, including:
  • Town Hall Meetings with Council Members to hear residents’ thoughts on the
  future of the community;
  • Public Safety Town Hall Meetings;
  • Sidewalk Improvement Project Town Hall;
  • Monterey Park Going Green survey, outreach, and public workshops to evaluate
  programs and plans for the City’s efforts in sustainability; and
  • Our City, Our Plan outreach workshop about downtown revitalization, housing
  opportunities and development streamlining.

When possible, the meetings listed above have been conducted in both virtual and in-
person platforms. In-person events were held at various locations around the City and
specifically included presentations that were held in areas that are categorized as a
disadvantaged community within the City.

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF MONTEREY
  PARK, CALIFORNIA, DECLARING AND RECOGNIZING THE MONTH
  OF MARCH 2024 AS AMERICAN RED CROSS MONTH

  BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Monterey Park as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follows:

  A. Clarissa (Clara) Harlowe Barton is one of the most honored women in American
  history known for her astounding devotion and dedication to helping others. Barton
  is considered a visionary whose humanitarian spirit helped change the world, and
  on May 21, 1881, founded the American Red Cross.

  B. After hearing of the Swiss-inspired global Red Cross network while visiting Europe
  following the Civil War, Barton and a few of her acquaintances campaigned for an
  American Red Cross and ratification of the Geneva Convention protecting the war-
  injured, which the United States ratified in 1882.

  C. Barton led the American Red Cross for 23 years and conducted its very first
  domestic and overseas disaster relief efforts. The American Red Cross also aided
  the U.S. military during the Spanish-American War and successfully campaigned
  for the inclusion of peacetime relief work as part of the global Red Cross network.

  D. The American Red Cross introduced its first aid, water safety, and public health
  nursing program prior to World War I, and by 1918, local chapters grew from 107
  to 3,864 with more than 30 million adult and junior Red Cross members. Following
  the war, the Red Cross focused its service to veterans and enhanced its programs
  in safety training, accident prevention, in-home care, and nutrition education.

  E. Extensive services provided by the American Red Cross were once again needed
  for the U.S. military in World War II. This request initiated a national blood program
  that collected 13.3 million pints of blood for use by the armed forces. Following
  World War II, the Red Cross introduced the first nationwide civilian blood program
  that now supplies more than 40% of the blood and blood products in the United
  States today.

  F. The American Red Cross has since expanded its services to include civil defense,
  CPR/AED training, HIV/AIDS education, and the provision of emotional care and
  support in the wake of disasters and continues to assist government agencies and
  community organizations plan, coordinate and provide feeding, sheltering, and
  family reunification services for people affected by disasters.

  G. Today, the American Red Cross provides compassionate care in five critical areas:
  people affected by disasters in America; support for members of the military and
  their families; blood collection, processing, and distribution; health and safety
  education and training; and international relief and development.

  Page 251 of 255
   H. Since 1943, every United States President regardless of political party has issued
  messages and proclamations recognizing the tremendous efforts made by the
  American Red Cross including providing aid during disasters, ensuring access to
  lifesaving blood, providing education and training, and alleviating human suffering
  in the face of emergencies by mobilizing the power of volunteers and the
  generosity of donors.

  I. The annual theme for American Red Cross Month is to honor those who deliver
  care and hope when help cannot wait during emergencies. In addition, March 27,
  2024, is designated as Red Cross Giving Day which aims to rally supporters
  nationwide to help provide shelter, food, relief items, emotional support, and other
  assistance for people affected by disasters.

  J. The Monterey Park City Council recognizes the compassion of people in the
  Monterey Park community and reaffirms their commitment to care for one another
  in times of crisis. Kindhearted individuals in Monterey Park exemplify Barton’s
  commitment as they step up through humanitarian efforts to provide a beacon of
  hope for those in need. Their voluntary and selfless contributions make a lifesaving
  difference and strengthen the Monterey Park community.

  K. The Monterey Park City Council hereby proclaims March 2024 as American Red
  Cross Month and encourages all residents of Monterey Park to reach out and
  support its humanitarian mission whether it is volunteering, donating blood, giving
  financially, or saving a life with first aid and CPR skills.

signatures in accordance with Government Code §16.5. Such electronic signatures will
be treated in all respects as having the same effect as an original signature.

Resolution, signifying its adoption by the City Council of the City of Monterey Park, and
the City Clerk, or her duly appointed deputy, may attest thereto.

SECTION 4: Effective Date. This Resolution will become effective immediately upon
adoption and will remain effective unless repealed or superseded.

  A RESOLUTION OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF MONTEREY
  PARK, CALIFORNIA, DECLARING AND RECOGNIZING THE MONTH
  OF MARCH 2024 AS WOMEN’S HISTORY MONTH, A NATIONAL
  CELEBRATION THAT HIGHLIGHTS THE CONTRIBUTIONS OF WOMEN
  TO EVENTS IN HISTORY AND CONTEMPORARY SOCIETY

  BE IT RESOLVED by the Council of the City of Monterey Park as follows:

SECTION 1: The City Council finds as follows:

  A. In February 1980, President Jimmy Carter issued a presidential proclamation
  declaring the week of March 8 as National Women’s History Week. The
  proclamation stated, “From the first settlers who came to our shores, from the first
  American Indian families who befriended them, men and women have worked
  together to build this nation. Too often the women were unsung and sometimes
  their contributions went unnoticed. However, the achievements, leadership,
  courage, strength, and love of the women who built America were as vital as that
  of the men whose names we know so well.”

  B. Women’s History Month originated as a national celebration in 1981 when
  Congress passed Public Law 97-28 which authorized the President to proclaim the
  week beginning March 7, 1982, as Women’s History Week. Throughout the next
  five years, Congress continued to pass joint resolutions designating a week in
  March as Women’s History Week.

  C. In 1987, after being petitioned by the National Women’s History Project, Congress
  passed Public Law 100-9 which designed the month of March 1987 as Women’s
  History Month.

  D. Between 1988 and 1994, Congress passed additional resolutions requesting and
  authorizing the President to proclaim March of each year as Women’s History
  Month. Since 1995, U.S. Presidents, regardless of political party, have issued a
  series of annual proclamations designating the month of March as Women’s
  History Month. These proclamations celebrate the contributions women have
  made and recognize the specific achievements women have made throughout
  American history in a variety of fields.

  E. Women’s History Month corresponds with International Women’s Day which is
  celebrated on March 8 worldwide. It provides an opportunity to celebrate the
  achievements of women while calling for greater equality.

  F. The National Women’s History Alliance designates a yearly theme for Women’s
  History Month. The 2024 theme celebrates “Women Who Advocate for Equity,
  Diversity and Inclusion” and recognizes women who understand the need to
  eliminate bias and discrimination from individuals’ lives and institutions.

  Page 253 of 255
 G. American women of every race, class, and ethnic background served as early
  leaders in the forefront of every major progressive social change movement.

H. American women have played and continue to play a critical economic, cultural,
  and social role in every sphere of the life of the nation by constituting a significant
  portion of the labor force working inside and outside of the home.

I. American women have served our country courageously in the military.

J. American women have been leaders, not only in securing their own rights of
  suffrage and equal opportunity, but also in the abolitionist movement, the
  emancipation movement, the industrial labor movement, the civil rights movement,
  and other movements, especially the peace movement, which create a more fair
  and just society for all.

K. In Monterey Park, 51.4% of all residents are female. Women of all backgrounds
  and ethnicities have made incredible impacts on our City. Some notable women in
  Monterey Park include:

  Laura C. Scudder, who in 1926, started Laura Scudder’s in Monterey Park,
  making potato chips. Scudder was described as ahead of her time, she was
  an entrepreneur, inventor, and doer. Most notably she introduced wax paper
  bags as a packaging solution for potato chips. Laura Scudder’s was also
  credited as the first company to imprint a freshness date on their food
  products, once again setting the standard, which is now mandatory for
  today’s food products.

  Lily Lee Chen, who on April 13, 1982, was elected to the City Council of
  Monterey Park and who made history in 1984 by becoming the first female
  Chinese American Mayor in the nation.

  - Randye Kay spoke about the traffic issues at Chandler and Hellman Avenues. She
  asked for active traffic enforcement to reduce pedestrian accidents and injuries.
  Ms. Kay spoke about the Metro Nashville Police Department who embarked on a
  traffic study in 2017 entitled “The Effect of High Visibility Enforcement on Motor
  Vehicle Crashes” which she said was published online by the National Institute of
  Justice. She said the study targeted the reduction of crashes at specific locations
  based on identifying behaviors. She stated the short-term decrease in accidents
  at specific targeted police interventions, successfully reduced crashes. Ms. Kay
  voiced her opinion that reducing accidents at the intersection of Chandler and
  Hellman Avenues requires structural and behavioral interventions, including no
  parking on both sides of Hellman, extension of red zones, and multiple stop signs.

  It is recommended that City Council waive the fare to the Spirit Bus on Monday,
  April 22, 2024, when Earth Day will be celebrated globally. Free rides on the Spirit
  Bus will promote public transportation and reduce traffic and the City’s carbon
  footprint through the reduction of automobile emissions. This action will support
  the City’s Going Green initiative to encourage the community to consider
  environmentally friendly activities such as using alternative forms of transportation.
  The Spirit Bus fare was also waived last year in honor of Earth Day 2023.
